---
description: "Use when editing cookbook rendering, print CSS, page layouts, the layout manifest, image placement, or generated image crops."
applyTo: ["src/family_cookbook/**", "examples/**/book/book.yaml", "examples/**/book/**/images/**"]

# Cookbook Layout And Rendering

- `src/family_cookbook/render.py` owns book order, page categories, rendering, print CSS, the generated pages (title page, contents, contributors, index), and centered page numbers. The contents, contributors, and index paginate in Python — `paginate()` packs rows into two columns per leaf using heights measured from the fonts (`REF_STYLES`, which also emits their CSS) — so their leaf count is settled before pages are numbered and they never take a FIT_SCRIPT zoom.
- `book/book.yaml` carries the book's structure (chapters, order, labels, accents), its identity and cover copy, and the `layouts:` list of curated archetypes and image zones. Entries absent from `layouts:` are auto-assigned at build time.
- Page geometry and fonts deliberately stay in `src/family_cookbook/render.py` — they satisfy the vendor spec in `docs/PRINTING.md` and are gated by `src/family_cookbook/check.py` (`cookbook check`), so they are not per-book settings. The geometry is single-sourced there: `PRINT_PAGE_W_IN`/`PRINT_PAGE_H_IN` and `PRINT_BLEED_IN` for the press page box, and the text block's distance from the trim in both builds — `MARGIN_IN` (0.75 in) at the top, outside, and inside (`PRINT_INSIDE_MARGIN_IN`, checked against Lulu's gutter table), `MARGIN_BOTTOM_IN` (0.875 in) at the foot, the folio `FOLIO_IN` (0.5 in) above the trim. `mode_vars_css()`, `TEXT_COLUMN_IN`, `TEXT_AREA_IN`, the photo frames, and the reference-page frame (`REF_FRAME_W`/`REF_FRAME_H`) derive from them. A margin change moves every text measure, so recalibrate everything below that is marked as measured: the `BAND_*` text model and `HERO_PANEL_IN`, `SIDEBAR_HEADER_IN`, `FULL_TYPE_LINES`, `PROSE_PAGE_LINES`, and the inset rule.
- `src/family_cookbook/fit_images.py` (`cookbook fit`) derives `{slug}-{sidebar|spread}.jpg` from canonical `images/{slug}.jpg`, one per fixed-size frame in `PHOTO_FRAMES` (`src/family_cookbook/render.py`). Never hand-edit derived crops.
- Band and hero photos are flexible: they take all the height the text leaves on the page, within `PHOTO_RANGE` (band `BAND_MIN_IN`–`BAND_MAX_IN`, 3–6.75 in; hero `HERO_MIN_IN`–`HERO_MAX_IN`, 5–7.25 in), so a short recipe gets a big photo and no page ends in empty paper while its photo is cropped. They have no crop file. The page carries the canonical image with crop windows precomputed for a run of heights (`photo_windows()` → `data-windows`); after layout, FIT_SCRIPT's `framePhotos()` applies the window nearest the photo's measured aspect as CSS `object-view-box`. Python predicts that height with `photo_room()`, a text-height model (`band_room()` and its `BAND_*` constants) calibrated against the press build to within about a quarter inch; layout choice and `photo_fit()` use it. Recalibrate those constants when the band page's type or geometry changes. The Recipe Spread's photo works the same way in spirit: its height is whatever the flowed text leaves, so it uses the canonical image.
- Crops follow the dish, not a fixed gravity. `photo_subject()` finds it in the canonical photo — fine detail and saturation against the plain backdrop, damped where the color matches the photo's border — along with the dish's full extent and any flat canvas padding above or below the photo. The extent follows the photo's outlines out from the dish, bridging small breaks and joining a faint stand just below it, so a glass's rim, stem, and foot, a pint's head, or a cake's frosted crown count as dish even though they carry little color or texture. `subject_crop()` tightens a band or column frame to the dish plus `DISH_AIR` around it, never below `PRINT_PPI` (300 ppi) at the placed size; a full-bleed frame, or a dish too big to tighten around, takes the largest window, centering the dish where it fits and otherwise holding the most of the food — but never cutting through the subject's top, so a tall subject loses its foot instead. No window crosses a padding seam when it fits inside the photo proper. Every `<img>` also gets an `object-position` on the dish, so frames that `object-fit` trims further (the screen draft, the Recipe Spread photo) keep it in view. Detection results are cached in `draft/photo-subjects.json`; bump `SUBJECT_VERSION` when `detect_subject()` changes. A recipe's `- **Image position:** top|center|bottom` is a manual override that pins the vertical crop (no tightening); set it only for a photo the detection misjudges, after looking at the rendered page.
- Run `cookbook fit` after adding, replacing, or reassigning a canonical image. It lists crops below print resolution and every placed frame that breaks `photo_fit()`'s rules — a candidate for a regenerated photo, a `layouts:` row with a frame that suits it, or an `Image position`.
- Readability floor: no line of reading text — ingredient, direction, note, prose paragraph or list item — prints below 10 pt (computed size × FIT_SCRIPT zoom). `src/family_cookbook/check.py` (`cookbook check`) fails the print build on any page under it. A framed prose page (an entry or a chapter's own page) too long for one leaf at full size does not shrink: when its `_body_lines()` estimate passes `PROSE_PAGE_LINES` it continues on the next leaf (`prose_continues()`, `is_prose_cont`, `render_prose_cont()`), the same frame under a running head "{Title}, continued". FIT_SCRIPT's `flowProse()` fills the first frame block by block, measured in the browser, and splits the block that no longer fits — a paragraph only at a line boundary, a list between items — with at least two lines (two items) on each side; a heading stays with what follows it. Auto-assignment keeps to it: `assign_section()` only picks a one-page archetype that holds the recipe at full type (`holds_at_full_type()`) — a band or hero whose text leaves its photo at least the range's minimum (`photo_room()`), or a fixed layout whose `FULL_TYPE_LINES` budget holds the recipe's `_body_lines()` estimate (the sidebar also needs `SIDEBAR_MIN_LINES`, so its text column is not mostly empty). There is no dense layout with a thin photo strip: a recipe that would leave a band under 3 in takes two pages. A recipe that fits none takes two facing pages, its first leaf always on an even page: the **Two-Page Spread** (photo full-bleed on the verso, the whole recipe on the recto) when it has a photo and fits that recipe leaf's budget, else the **Recipe Spread** — both pages one four-column grid, title block on the verso, ingredients → directions → notes flowed column by column by FIT_SCRIPT's `flow()` step in the browser (never splitting an item, headings and subheads kept with their first item), the photo taking the height left at the foot of the recto, or a band under the verso title when that is under 2.5 in. A curated `layouts:` row is not checked against the budgets, so confirm it with `src/family_cookbook/check.py` (`cookbook check`). Recalibrate `FULL_TYPE_LINES` whenever page geometry or an archetype's type changes: render every recipe in every archetype in the print build, measure the zoom FIT_SCRIPT would need, and set each budget just under the lowest estimate of any page that would print under 10 pt.
- The photo must show the dish, not the photo's whole frame. `photo_fit()` judges the food (`Subject.box`, the detailed, edible mass) apart from the subject (`Subject.extent`, the food with its glass, mug, stand, plate, or pan). Any frame may crop a vessel's side or a plate's edge, as food photography does, but never cuts through the subject's top — a glass's rim, a pint's head, a cake's crown, a bowl's rim — so a tall subject loses its foot instead. The hero and spread must show `FOOD_WHOLE` (0.7) of the food's width and height, measured on a box that runs past the food's visible edge, so in practice the whole food. The band, judged at its predicted height, must hold `BAND_FOOD_HELD` (0.55) of the food's detail mass — a short band may trim the outer edge of a deep dish, never its body. The sidebar must show `COLUMN_FOOD` (0.9) of the food's width with the dish filling at least `COLUMN_FILL` (half) of the column — so it takes only genuinely narrow, standing subjects (a glass, a mug). A standing subject (one the sidebar frames whole) also keeps `STANDING_WHOLE` (0.9) of its silhouette, foot included, in the other frames. Auto-assignment skips a frame that breaks these rules. A photo never costs a page: when a recipe's text fits one-page layouts but its photo suits none of their frames, it takes the band or hero showing the most food, and `cookbook fit` reports it as a candidate for a regenerated photo. A two-page layout is chosen only for text length or by a curated `layouts:` row. Recalibrate the thresholds by eye — render every photo in every frame — if frames or `detect_subject()` change.
- `extras/` keepsakes are never cropped or fitted: they print whole, at their own aspect ratio. `place_extras()` in `src/family_cookbook/render.py` decides placement in Python before rendering — an inset on a Text-Only Framed page whose estimated body fits `INSET_ROOM`, or on a Half-Page Classic page whose band keeps its minimum after giving up `INSET_IN` (`inset_has_room()`), otherwise a keepsake page (`is_keepsake`) right after the entry (after both leaves of a two-page recipe), with a folio and no contents/index line. A `layouts:` row may force it with `extras: inset` or `extras: page`. Recalibrate `INSET_ROOM` and `INSET_IN` if those archetypes' geometry changes — render every candidate page with an inset of one and of two items in both builds: an inset must never make FIT_SCRIPT zoom a page.
- Both builds paginate like the bound book (`insert_recto_blanks()`), and the screen draft lays pages out as facing spreads; print media keeps one page per sheet. Use `cookbook build --only slug1,slug2` for focused visual checks — a two-page recipe still shows as its spread. It replaces `draft/cookbook-draft.html` with just those entries; run `cookbook build` again for the whole book.
- Inspect rendered output after content or renderer changes; the parser and layout engine can drop or clip content that looks valid in Markdown.
